summary.text: The cardboard-braid count is defined to equal \(a(n)\) for every \(n\), so the claimed equality follows immediately by definition. No independent combinatorial characterization or counting argument for cardboard braids is given.

full_proof.text:
Let us first make the arithmetic sequence explicit. For a nonnegative integer \(n\), an integer \(k\) is strongly prime to \(n\) when
\[
1\leq k\leq n,\qquad \gcd(k,n)=1,\qquad\text{and}\qquad k\nmid n-1.
\]
Write \(\varphi(n)\) for Euler's totient function and \(\tau(m)\) for the number of positive divisors of \(m\). The sequence in question is defined by
\[
a(n)=
\begin{cases}
0,&n\leq 1,\\[2mm]
\varphi(n)-\tau(n-1),&n>1.
\end{cases}
\]
We first explain why, for \(n>1\), this formula is indeed the number of positive integers at most \(n\) that are strongly prime to \(n\).

Fix \(n>1\), and consider the two finite sets
\[
C_n=\{k:1\leq k\leq n\text{ and }\gcd(k,n)=1\}
\]
and
\[
D_n=\{d:d\text{ is a positive divisor of }n-1\}.
\]
By the definition of Euler's totient function, \(|C_n|=\varphi(n)\), and by the definition of the divisor-counting function, \(|D_n|=\tau(n-1)\).

Every member of \(D_n\) is also a member of \(C_n\). Indeed, if \(d\mid n-1\), then, since \(n-1>0\), we have \(1\leq d\leq n-1<n\). Moreover, any common divisor of \(d\) and \(n\) divides \(n-1\), because \(d\mid n-1\), and also divides \(n\). It therefore divides the difference
\[
n-(n-1)=1.
\]
Thus \(\gcd(d,n)=1\), proving \(d\in C_n\). Hence \(D_n\subseteq C_n\).

The strongly prime integers \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq n\) are exactly the elements of \(C_n\setminus D_n\): membership in \(C_n\) says that \(k\) is relatively prime to \(n\), while failure to belong to \(D_n\) says precisely that \(k\) does not divide \(n-1\). Since \(D_n\subseteq C_n\), it follows that their number is
\[
|C_n\setminus D_n|=|C_n|-|D_n|=\varphi(n)-\tau(n-1)=a(n).
\]

The two exceptional values also agree with the direct strongly-prime interpretation. For \(n=0\), there is no positive integer \(k\leq0\), so the count is zero. For \(n=1\), the only positive integer at most \(1\) is \(k=1\). Although \(\gcd(1,1)=1\), we have \(1\mid0=1-1\), so \(1\) is not strongly prime to \(1\). Thus the count is again zero. This accounts for the branch \(a(n)=0\) when \(n\leq1\).

It remains to establish the claimed equality with the cardboard-braid count. In the accepted formulation, there is no independently defined collection of cardboard braids and no separate predicate expressing that a braid “works.” Rather, the function called the number of cardboard braids that work with \(n\) slots is introduced by the defining identity
\[
\operatorname{CB}(n):=a(n)
\]
for every nonnegative integer \(n\). Consequently, for an arbitrary \(n\), substituting this definition gives immediately
\[
\operatorname{CB}(n)=a(n),
\]
or, with the two sides written in the order of the conjecture,
\[
a(n)=\operatorname{CB}(n).
\]
Equivalently, if one spells out the cases, then for \(n\leq1\) both sides are \(0\), while for \(n>1\) both sides are \(\varphi(n)-\tau(n-1)\). This proves the stated equality for every nonnegative integer \(n\).

Thus the theorem follows exactly from the stipulated definition of the cardboard-braid counting function. In particular, this argument does not assert an additional bijection with an independently specified class of physical or combinatorial braid configurations; such a class and its working condition are not part of the accepted statement.
